steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from the 'react' module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing from a package
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have access to React and the useState hook for building components with state.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create a parent component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named ParentComponent that returns an empty div element.
steps.hint: Define a function called ParentComponent that returns JSX containing a <div> element.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create ParentComponent here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a ParentComponent function that returns an empty div.
successCriteria: ParentComponent is defined as a function and returns a <div> element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the ParentComponent.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure ParentComponent returns a <div> element.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've defined a function named ParentComponent that returns a div.

steps.title: Initialize state in the parent
steps.instruction: Inside ParentComponent, use useState to create a count state variable initialized to 0.
steps.hint: Call useState(0) and destructure the returned array into count and setCount variables.
steps.expectedOutcome: ParentComponent will have a count state variable that starts at 0.
successCriteria: ParentComponent contains a useState call that initializes count to 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've initialized the count state that will trigger re-renders.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using useState with an initial value of 0 inside ParentComponent.
steps.feedbackWrong: The count state isn't properly initialized. Check that you're using useState(0) inside ParentComponent.

steps.title: Create a child component without memo
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named ChildComponent that takes a prop called 'value' and renders it inside a paragraph element.
steps.hint: Define a component that accepts props and returns JSX with a paragraph containing the prop value.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a ChildComponent function that renders a paragraph with the 'value' prop.
successCriteria:
ChildComponent is defined as a function that takes a 'value' prop and returns

{value}

.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a simple child component that will help demonstrate unnecessary re-renders.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure ChildComponent accepts a 'value' prop and renders it inside a paragraph.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the component definition. It should be a function named ChildComponent that takes a 'value' prop and returns a paragraph with that value.

steps.title: Render the child in the parent
steps.instruction: Inside the ParentComponent's return statement, render the ChildComponent and pass a static prop named 'message' with the value 'Hello'.
steps.hint: Add <ChildComponent message="Hello" /> inside the return statement of ParentComponent.
steps.expectedOutcome: The parent component will now render the child component with a static prop.
successCriteria: ChildComponent is rendered inside ParentComponent's JSX with a prop named 'message' set to 'Hello'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully rendered the child component from the parent with a static prop.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're rendering ChildComponent inside ParentComponent's return statement and passing a prop named 'message' with value 'Hello'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't match what we need. Look at the hint and try again.

steps.title: Add a button to update parent state
steps.instruction: Inside the ParentComponent, add a button element with the text 'Increment count' that calls a function to increment the count state when clicked.
steps.hint: Create an onClick handler that uses the setCount function to update the state. You can use an arrow function directly in the onClick attribute.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: button that increments a counter
<button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>Increment</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The ParentComponent will have a button that increments the count state when clicked, demonstrating how parent state changes trigger re-renders.
successCriteria: A button element with text 'Increment count' is added inside ParentComponent's return, and its onClick handler increments the count state.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a button that updates the parent state. This will help demonstrate re-renders in the next steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but make sure it has the correct text 'Increment count' and properly increments the count state when clicked.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or doesn't increment the count state correctly. Check that you've added the button inside ParentComponent and used setCount to update the state.

steps.title: Add console logs to observe renders
steps.instruction: Inside the ParentComponent, add a console.log statement that logs 'Parent rendered' when it renders. Inside the ChildComponent, add a console.log statement that logs 'Child rendered' when it renders.
steps.hint: Place console.log statements directly in the component body, before the return statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: Both components will log messages to the console when they render, allowing you to observe re-renders.
successCriteria: ParentComponent logs 'Parent rendered' and ChildComponent logs 'Child rendered' to the console when they render.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added console logs to both components. Now you can see in the console when each component renders.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added console logs, but make sure both components have them. Check that ParentComponent logs 'Parent rendered' and ChildComponent logs 'Child rendered'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The console logs are missing or incorrect. Add console.log statements inside both ParentComponent and ChildComponent to log when they render.

steps.title: Wrap ChildComponent with React.memo
steps.instruction: Wrap the existing ChildComponent with React.memo to prevent unnecessary re-renders.
steps.hint: Use React.memo to wrap the component definition. This will memoize the component and only re-render when its props change.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: wrapping a component with React.memo
const MemoizedComponent = React.memo(Component);
steps.expectedOutcome: The ChildComponent will be wrapped with React.memo, which will optimize performance by preventing re-renders when its props haven't changed.
successCriteria: ChildComponent is wrapped with React.memo and the component is properly memoized.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully wrapped ChildComponent with React.memo. This will prevent unnecessary re-renders when the parent component updates but the child's props remain the same.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're wrapping the entire ChildComponent with React.memo. Check that you're using the correct syntax: React.memo(ChildComponent).
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't properly wrapped with React.memo. Remember to use React.memo to wrap the component definition.

steps.title: Observe the memoization effect
steps.instruction: Click the increment button in the browser preview and check the console to see that only ParentComponent logs appear.
steps.hint: Open your browser's developer tools console (F12 or right-click → Inspect → Console) before clicking the button.
steps.expectedOutcome: When you click the increment button, the console should show 'ParentComponent renders' but not 'ChildComponent renders', demonstrating that React.memo prevents unnecessary re-renders.
successCriteria: Only ParentComponent logs appear in the console when the button is clicked
ChildComponent does not log on subsequent clicks
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've observed that React.memo prevents ChildComponent from re-rendering when its props don't change, even though ParentComponent's state updates.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your console output carefully. You should see 'ParentComponent renders' but not 'ChildComponent renders' when clicking the button.
steps.feedbackWrong: Make sure you've wrapped ChildComponent with React.memo and that you're checking the console output after clicking the button.

steps.title: Add a dynamic prop to bypass memo
steps.instruction: Pass the count state as a prop to ChildComponent so it receives a changing value on each button click.
steps.hint: Add the count variable as a prop when rendering ChildComponent in ParentComponent's JSX.
steps.analogousExample:
// Passing dynamic prop to a component
<DisplayItem value={currentValue} />
steps.expectedOutcome: ChildComponent will now re-render with each button click because it receives a changing prop, demonstrating that React.memo doesn't prevent re-renders when props change.
successCriteria: ChildComponent receives the count prop from ParentComponent.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully passed the count state as a prop to ChildComponent. Now when you click the button, ChildComponent will re-render each time because its props are changing, showing that React.memo only prevents unnecessary re-renders when props stay the same.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're passing the count variable as a prop to ChildComponent. Look at how the message prop is passed and add a similar prop for count.
steps.feedbackWrong: The count prop needs to be passed from ParentComponent to ChildComponent. In ParentComponent's JSX, add count={count} to the ChildComponent element.
